title: Supporting the Uptake of Evidence-Based Care for Degenerative Meniscal Tears and Early Knee Osteoarthritis: A Collaborative Approach to the Development of an Intervention Using Stakeholder Perspectives and Integrating Behaviour Change Theory

sections.title: 研究问题
sections.text:
《Supporting the Uptake of Evidence-Based Care for Degenerative Meniscal Tears and Early Knee Osteoarthritis: A Collaborative Approach to the Development of an Intervention Using Stakeholder Perspectives and Integrating Behaviour Change Theory》：研究问题的原文依据。

【Background · hex70940-sec-0060-p3】Imaging findings have limited relevance to management in early‐stage knee OA [7, 18]. Despite this, inappropriate use of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to investigate knee pain in middle‐aged and older adults, without a history of trauma or red flags, is well documented, both in Ireland and internationally [19, 20, 21, 22], and continues to rise [23]. Overuse of diagnostic imaging has been implicated in driving patients with DMT, and their healthcare professionals (HCPs), to seek early orthopaedic or surgical solutions [24, 25, 26], and has been implicated in persistently high knee arthroscopy rates in some countries [26, 27]. Arthroscopic surgery, or partial meniscectomy, as a treatment of DMT is no more effective than sham surgery for improving pain and reducing disability [28, 29], and several studies have associated this procedure with a higher risk of OA progression [30, 31, 32]. Importantly, continued use of ‘unnecessary interventions’ for knee OA, such as MRI and arthroscopy, does not appear to translate into better clinical outcomes [23, 33] and their overuse has important resource implications, further underscoring the need to reduce mismanagement and low‐value care [34, 35].

【Background · hex70940-sec-0060-p8】While the strong recommendations against surgery for degenerative meniscal pathology are gradually translating to practice [55, 56, 57], uncertainty remains regarding how best to implement conservative management, particularly for people with DMT and early OA. Recent evidence indicates that implementation of recommended OA care is influenced by interacting barriers at patient, HCP, service and health‐system levels [45, 58]. To our knowledge, no theory‐informed intervention with stakeholder involvement has been developed that specifically targets people with DMT and early OA changes and/or their healthcare providers. This study aims to describe the systematic development of a multifaceted implementation intervention to improve the delivery and uptake of evidence‐based care for people with DMTs and early knee OA.

sections.title: 研究方法
sections.text:
《Supporting the Uptake of Evidence-Based Care for Degenerative Meniscal Tears and Early Knee Osteoarthritis: A Collaborative Approach to the Development of an Intervention Using Stakeholder Perspectives and Integrating Behaviour Change Theory》：方法与研究设计的原文依据。

【Design and Setting · hex70940-sec-0080-p1】We used a four‐step approach, consisting of guiding questions, first described by French et al., to structure the intervention development process (Figure 1) [59]. This approach combines behavioural change theory, stakeholder involvement and evidence on intervention effectiveness. For further guidance, we also drew on case examples that outlined their use of this four‐step development process [49, 60]. The process is reported in line with the Guidance for the Reporting of Intervention Development (GUIDED) checklist [61]. The Guidance for Reporting Involvement of Patients and the Public (GRIPP) 2 short form (SF) reporting guideline checklist [62] was also followed. Both reporting guidelines are presented in Supplementary File 1. The research team provided expertise in knee OA, general practice, orthopaedics, qualitative, health services research and designing behavioural theory informed interventions to the development process.

【Design and Setting · hex70940-sec-0080-p2】This intervention development study is part of the Knowledge translation and Exercise for Degenerative Meniscal Pathology and Early osteoarthritis (KNEE‐DEeP) project, which builds on earlier studies [25, 43, 44], with plans to test the intervention in a future KNEE‐DEeP feasibility study [63]. The project is set in the Southwest region of Ireland, where people with knee pain access a mixed public–private system of healthcare. The number of people paying for private health insurance is substantial, estimated to be 48% of the population. Publicly funded physiotherapy is delivered by the Health Services Executive (HSE), but long waiting times can hinder access, and not all patients are entitled to this service [64]. Approximately 42% of the Irish population has access to free GP care [65]. Patients without entitlement to public physiotherapy or free GP care pay out‐of‐pocket [66].

sections.title: 主要结果
sections.text:
《Supporting the Uptake of Evidence-Based Care for Degenerative Meniscal Tears and Early Knee Osteoarthritis: A Collaborative Approach to the Development of an Intervention Using Stakeholder Perspectives and Integrating Behaviour Change Theory》：结果的原文依据；数值与适用人群以引文为准。

【Summary of Main Findings · hex70940-sec-0340-p1】This study describes the systematic development of a multi‐level, theory‐informed implementation intervention designed to improve evidence‐based management of DMT and early knee OA. By integrating behavioural theory, stakeholder input and empirical evidence, our intervention directly addresses well‐documented evidence–practice gaps in the conservative management of degenerative knee conditions.

【Conclusion · hex70940-sec-0380-p1】Using a systematic, theory‐informed and stakeholder‐engaged approach, we developed a multifaceted intervention to support delivery and uptake of evidence‐based care for DMT and early knee OA. The intervention comprised small‐group educational workshops and resources for GPs to support the delivery of an ‘enhanced consultation’, with the facility to refer patients for an early ‘best practice’ physiotherapy session. The patient intervention, therefore, consisted of two key components: an ‘enhanced consultation’ with the GP followed by a ‘best practice’ physiotherapy session. This single session delivers individualised education and a bespoke exercise and physical activity plan to boost self‐management and self‐efficacy. The resulting intervention requires testing to explore its acceptability, feasibility and suitability for scale‐up in clinical practice.
